holidays.name: National Puzzle Day
holidays.description: A day for jigsaws, crosswords, Sudoku, Rubik's Cubes, and anything else that makes your brain squirm. Puzzle lovers are encouraged to spend the day solving something tricky, ideally while ignoring all other responsibilities.
holidays.origin: Created in 2002 by Jodi Jill, a puzzle enthusiast and author who wanted to celebrate the mental benefits of puzzles and encourage people to give their brains a workout.
holidays.funFact: The first jigsaw puzzle was made around 1760 by London mapmaker John Spilsbury, who glued a map to wood and cut out the countries to teach geography.

holidays.name: National Corn Chip Day
holidays.description: A salute to the crunchy, salty, scoop-friendly snack that makes dips, chili, and nachos possible. Grab a bag, crack open some salsa, and crunch responsibly.
holidays.origin: The date is tied to the popularization of corn chips in the 1930s, when Texan Charles Elmer Doolin began mass-producing them and launched the Fritos brand. The day itself is an unofficial food observance.
holidays.funFact: Doolin reportedly bought the original corn chip recipe and a small potato-ricer for $100 in 1932, using money borrowed from his mother, who pawned her wedding ring.

holidays.name: Freethinkers Day
holidays.description: An observance for skeptics, rationalists, and independent thinkers to celebrate reason, free inquiry, and questioning everything, including whether you should celebrate a holiday at all.
holidays.origin: It is observed on January 29 in honor of the birthday of Thomas Paine, the Enlightenment-era author of Common Sense, who was born in 1737. Freethought groups have marked the day to celebrate his advocacy of reason and liberty.
holidays.funFact: Common Sense sold an estimated 500,000 copies in colonial America, which is a staggering number for a population of about 2.5 million people.

holidays.name: National Hot Chocolate Day
holidays.description: A cozy day for sipping rich, steamy cocoa in the middle of winter. Marshmallows, whipped cream, peppermint sticks, and tiny cookie dunks are all strongly encouraged.
holidays.origin: An unofficial food observance placed in late January when winter is at its coldest in the Northern Hemisphere, making it a perfect time to celebrate cocoa. Its roots trace back to ancient Mesoamerican chocolate drinks, which were originally enjoyed cold and bitter.
holidays.funFact: The Maya and Aztecs drank chocolate as a frothy, spicy beverage, and Aztec ruler Montezuma was said to drink it from golden cups.

holidays.name: Curmudgeons Day
holidays.description: A day dedicated to grumpy people everywhere. Complain freely, grumble at the weather, and mutter about how things were better in the old days. No one is allowed to tell you to cheer up.
holidays.origin: Curmudgeons Day is an unofficial humor observance that traditionally falls on January 29, giving the world's professional grouches a day to be proudly cranky.
holidays.funFact: The word curmudgeon has uncertain origins, but it has been used in English since the 16th century to describe a bad-tempered or stubborn person.
